covered: The problem of indirect knowledge: Kola borehole at 12.26 km against a 6,371 km radius; the four witnesses (density, seismic waves, gravity, meteorites).
The density argument: crustal rock 2.7–3.0 g/cm³ against a mean Earth density of about 5.5 g/cm³.

Chemical layering: oceanic crust (5–10 km, basaltic, ~3.0) versus continental crust (30–70 km, granitic, ~2.7); SiAl and SiMa; mantle to 2,900 km, peridotite, solid but plastic; core as NIFE, outer liquid, inner solid.
Discontinuities: Moho (crust–mantle), Gutenberg (mantle–core), Lehmann (outer–inner core), with Conrad mentioned only in passing.
Seismic waves: P (longitudinal, fastest, all media), S (transverse, solids only), L (surface, slowest, most destructive).
Shadow zones: S-wave shadow beyond 103°; P-wave shadow 103°–142°; P waves returning beyond 142° via inner-core refraction. The nesting of the P shadow inside the S shadow was emphasised.

Why the outer core is liquid and the inner core solid: pressure at the inner-core boundary around 330 GPa raising the melting point of iron above the ambient temperature; the geodynamo and the growing inner core.
Lithosphere versus asthenosphere as a mechanical rather than chemical division; the low-velocity zone; the lithosphere as the plate.

Isostasy: Airy (uniform density, variable thickness, roots) versus Pratt (variable density, uniform depth of compensation); Himalayan crustal root, Ganga plain flexure, Peninsular shield rigidity, post-glacial rebound in Scandinavia and Canada.
The geoid: equipotential surface at mean sea level, departures of up to about ±100 m from the WGS84 ellipsoid, orthometric versus ellipsoidal heights, and the Indian Ocean Geoid Low at roughly 106 m.
lastHandoff.next: Continental Drift to Plate Tectonics: A Theory That Changed Everything — Wegener's continental drift and its evidence (jigsaw fit, fossils, rocks, palaeoclimate); why drift was rejected; sea-floor spreading and magnetic striping; Harry Hess and the 1960s revolution; plate boundaries (divergent, convergent, transform); mantle convection; hotspots.
lastHandoff.notes: Three new reusable figures were created here. 'earth-interior' is the master cut-away and should be reused whenever the internal structure, discontinuities or core composition come up — including in the plate tectonics lesson and in any question on the geodynamo or the magnetic field. 'seismic-shadow-zones' is reusable for earthquake seismology, for the structure of the Earth, and for any question on how geophysicists image the interior; it pairs naturally with the earth-interior figure. 'isostasy-airy' is reusable for the Himalaya, for the Ganga basin, for post-glacial rebound, for gravity anomalies and for the broader theme of crustal compensation. The Inge Lehmann anecdote is a strong Indian-classroom-friendly story about women in science and about inference from absence — it can be reused in the history-of-science overlap and in essay openings. The Kola borehole figure (12.26 km against 6,371 km) is a good hook and can be reused in any lesson on the scale of the Earth. Deliberately NOT done here: the latitude-belts figure from Lesson 2 was not rebuilt, and the 'map as argument' stance from Lesson 1 was not re-established. The Coriolis preview from Lesson 4 was not paid off here — it still belongs to the atmospheric circulation lesson, where the pressure-gradient force, geostrophic balance and the three-cell model need the full treatment. The sun-synchronous orbit hook from Lesson 4 also remains open for the remote sensing or climatology unit. The next teacher should open by connecting the rigid lithosphere and plastic asthenosphere directly to the idea of mobile plates — that is the bridge into Wegener.
